questions.q: What does SQLAlchemy's create_engine() actually do?
options: Immediately opens and holds one database connection forever
Builds a reusable connection object that opens connections as needed
Replaces pyodbc entirely with a new driver
Deletes any existing tables at the target database
questions.explain: create_engine() doesn't connect right away - it builds a reusable Engine object.

questions.q: What does pyodbc have to do with SQLAlchemy in this lesson's setup?
options: Nothing - SQLAlchemy replaces pyodbc entirely
SQLAlchemy uses pyodbc underneath for the actual SQL Server connection
pyodbc is only used for writing, SQLAlchemy only for reading
They cannot be used in the same project
questions.explain: The mssql+pyodbc:// URL tells SQLAlchemy to use pyodbc as its underlying driver.

questions.q: What does df.to_sql() require that a raw pyodbc connection cannot directly provide?
options: A SQLAlchemy engine
A CSV file on disk
An internet connection
A pandas Series instead of a DataFrame
questions.explain: pandas' to_sql() method is built to work against a SQLAlchemy engine, not a raw pyodbc connection.

questions.q: What does if_exists="replace" do when calling df.to_sql()?
options: Appends new rows to the existing table
Raises an error if the table already exists
Drops and recreates the target table before writing
Ignores the write entirely
questions.explain: "replace" drops the table first; "append" adds rows; "fail" (the default) raises an error.

questions.q: When is it worth reaching for SQLAlchemy instead of raw pyodbc, per this lesson?
options: Only when writing single-row INSERT statements
Never - pyodbc should always be preferred
When using .to_sql() regularly, working across multiple database engines, or using an ORM
Only when the database has fewer than 10 tables
questions.explain: SQLAlchemy's extra setup pays off once you need to_sql(), multi-engine support, or an ORM.
